d.title: The test pyramid
d.caption: Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, a handful of end-to-end checks at the top. The shape is about cost: a unit test runs in microseconds and pins one decision; an end-to-end test runs in seconds and pins nothing in particular.

items.label: end-to-end
items.sub: a few · slow · the whole system

d.title: What pytest collects
d.caption: Files matching test_*.py or *_test.py, then functions starting with test_ and methods of classes starting with Test. Anything else is invisible, which is the usual reason a new test 'does not run'.

d.title: Fixtures form a dependency graph
d.caption: A test names the fixtures it needs; each fixture can name others. pytest builds them in dependency order, once per scope, and tears them down in reverse.

d.title: Stacked parametrize is a product
d.caption: Two @parametrize decorators multiply: three inputs by two modes is six test cases, each reported with its own id.

d.title: Patch where it is looked up, not where it is defined
d.caption: orders.py did 'from payments import charge', so it holds its own name 'charge'. Patching payments.charge changes a name orders never reads; patching orders.charge is what the test needs.

nodes.label: orders.charge
nodes.sub: bound at import — the name the code uses

d.title: Functional core, imperative shell
d.caption: Pure functions in the middle take data and return data — trivially testable. The thin shell around them does the I/O: reads the file, calls the API, writes the database. Tests target the core; a few integration tests cover the shell.

nodes.label: core: pure functions
nodes.sub: data in, data out — unit tested

d.title: Stub HTTP at the right layer
d.caption: Replace the transport, not your own client code: respx or a fake transport answers httpx's requests, so serialisation, retries and error handling still run for real.

d.title: Handling a flaky test
d.caption: A test that passes on retry is measuring something outside the code: time, ordering, shared state or the network. Quarantine it, find the dependency, remove it — never just add a retry.

items.label: Quarantine
items.desc: mark it, keep the suite green, keep it running

items.label: Find the hidden input
items.desc: clock, random seed, test order, shared fixture, real network

items.label: Make the input explicit
items.desc: freeze time, seed, isolate state, stub the network

items.label: Un-quarantine or delete
items.desc: a test nobody trusts is worse than no test

d.title: Growth classes at n = 1,000 and n = 1,000,000
d.caption: The constant does not matter; the column does. Quadratic at a million is a trillion steps — hours — which is why the accidental quadratic is the performance bug that reaches production.

d.title: Four instruments, four questions
d.caption: Pick the tool by the question. Each answers one thing well and the others badly.

columns.title: timeit
items: how long does this expression take?

columns.title: py-spy
items: what is the live process doing?

d.title: Where the bytes go
d.caption: An int is 28 bytes; a list of a million ints is 8 MB of pointers plus 28 MB of ints. The same numbers in a NumPy array are 8 MB total, and __slots__ removes the per-instance dict from objects.

d.title: lru_cache in front of a function
d.caption: The decorator keeps a dict from arguments to results. A hit returns without calling the function; a miss calls it and stores the result; at maxsize the least recently used entry is evicted. Arguments must be hashable.

d.title: N+1: one query per row
d.caption: Fetching 4 orders then each order's customer is 5 round trips; a join or a batched IN (...) is 1. At 400 orders the difference is 401 round trips against 1 — the same code, a hundred times slower.

d.title: Is it Python, and what then
d.caption: Profile first: most slow Python programs are slow because of an algorithm or I/O, not the interpreter. Only when the hot loop is genuinely numeric Python do the last three options apply.

items.label: Profile
items.desc: is the time in your loop, in a library, or waiting on I/O?

items.label: Fix the algorithm or the query
Vectorise
items.desc: NumPy, pandas, polars — the loop moves into C

items.label: Native code
items.desc: Cython, Rust via PyO3, a C extension

items.label: Scale out
items.desc: more processes or machines — after the above, not instead

d.title: Which model for which workload
d.caption: I/O-bound work waits; threads and asyncio overlap the waiting. CPU-bound work computes; only processes (or free-threaded Python) use a second core, because of the GIL.

cells.text: best at scale — one thread, thousands of tasks

d.title: Concurrency versus parallelism
d.caption: Two I/O tasks on one core interleave their waits and finish in about the time of one. Two CPU tasks on one core just take turns; they need two cores to finish sooner.

d.title: The GIL is released during blocking I/O
d.caption: A thread that calls into a socket read, file read, sleep or a C extension that releases the lock lets another thread run. A thread computing in pure Python holds the lock until the interpreter switches it out.

d.title: A race on counter += 1
d.caption: The += is three bytecodes: read, add, write. Two threads can both read 5, both write 6, and one increment is lost. A lock makes the three steps one.

d.title: Deadlock: two locks, two orders
d.caption: A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Neither can proceed. The fix is one global lock order — or one lock.

d.title: Crossing the process boundary
d.caption: Arguments are pickled, sent through a pipe, unpickled in the child; results come back the same way. A large array crosses twice, which is why multiprocessing loses on small tasks with big inputs.

d.title: submit and as_completed
d.caption: submit returns a Future immediately; the pool runs the callable on a worker; as_completed yields futures in the order they finish, not the order they were submitted.

d.title: The event loop
d.caption: One thread runs a loop: take a ready task, run it until it awaits something that is not ready, hand control back, check which I/O completed, mark those tasks ready. Nothing runs in parallel; everything takes turns at await points.

d.title: One blocking call stalls every task
d.caption: time.sleep(2) or a synchronous requests.get inside a coroutine holds the only thread; no other task runs until it returns. await asyncio.sleep or an async client yields instead.

d.title: gather versus TaskGroup
d.caption: gather runs coroutines concurrently and returns their results in order; if one fails the others keep running unless you cancel them. A TaskGroup cancels the siblings on the first failure and raises an ExceptionGroup — structured concurrency.

d.title: The procedure for choosing a model
d.caption: Answer the questions in order; the first yes decides. Most services end at step 2 or 3.

items.label: Is it CPU-bound Python?
items.desc: yes → multiprocessing (or native code); the GIL rules out threads

items.label: Is it I/O-bound with a few tasks?
items.desc: yes → ThreadPoolExecutor; simplest, works with any library

items.label: Is it I/O-bound with thousands of connections?
items.desc: yes → asyncio, with async libraries end to end

items.label: Is it mixed?
items.desc: asyncio for the I/O, run_in_executor or a process pool for the CPU parts

d.title: Safe and idempotent methods
d.caption: Safe: no state change. Idempotent: repeating has the same effect as doing it once. A client may retry idempotent requests freely; POST needs an idempotency key to be retried safely.

d.title: The defaults are the bugs
d.caption: requests.get(url) has no timeout, no retry policy and trusts whatever comes back. A production client sets a timeout, checks the status, retries only idempotent calls with backoff, and validates the body at the boundary.

d.title: Parse, don't validate
d.caption: Untrusted JSON enters, a Pydantic model parses it once at the boundary, and everything inside works with a typed object that cannot be malformed. Validation logic lives in one place instead of every function.

d.title: A FastAPI request, end to end
d.caption: The path is matched, parameters are parsed from the path, query and body according to the signature's annotations, dependencies run, the handler runs, and the return value is serialised through response_model.

d.title: Depends builds a graph per request
d.caption: A handler depends on a current user, which depends on a token, which depends on the request headers; a database session is shared by anything in the request that asks for it. FastAPI resolves the graph once per request and caches each node.

d.title: Middleware wraps every request
d.caption: Each middleware sees the request on the way in and the response on the way out, in nested order. Cross-cutting concerns — request IDs, timing, CORS — belong here; business logic does not.

d.title: Three ways to version an API
d.caption: Path versions are visible and cacheable; header versions keep URLs stable; additive change avoids versioning altogether for as long as it can.

d.title: Accept the work, return a job
d.caption: A slow operation should not hold an HTTP connection open. The handler validates, enqueues, and returns 202 with a job id; a worker does the work; the client polls or receives a webhook.

d.title: Storing and checking a password
d.caption: Never store the password; store a slow, salted hash. argon2 or bcrypt take tens of milliseconds by design, so a stolen table cannot be brute-forced quickly. Verification hashes the attempt with the stored salt and compares in constant time.

items.label: store the hash string only
items.desc: it contains the algorithm, parameters and salt

d.title: A JWT is three base64 parts
d.caption: header.payload.signature. The payload is readable by anyone — it is encoded, not encrypted — so it must not carry secrets. The signature is what the server checks; a token with alg 'none' or an unexpected algorithm must be rejected.
d.label: verify: the signature, the algorithm you expect, exp, iss and aud — every time
